sentences.text: Bajadasaurus was a large, four-legged herbivore with a long neck, tail, and small head.
Its neck featured extremely elongated, two-pronged neural spines extending outward.
The skull was slender and held about 48 pencil-shaped teeth located only at the front of the jaws.
Eye openings positioned high on the head allowed the animal to look forward while feeding.
The sole known specimen was dug up in 2010 by scientists from the Argentine National Scientific and Technical Research Council.
Argentine paleontologist Pablo Gallina discovered the fossil.
It was found at the Bajada Colorada locality, forty kilometers south of Picún Leufú near the Limay River.
The specimen is now kept at the Museo Municipal Ernesto Bachmann in Villa El Chocón, Neuquén Province, under catalog number MMCh-PV 75.
Muscle reconstructions suggest Bajadasaurus could not pull its head up as high as Camarasaurus, likely because it ate lower vegetation.
Garderes estimated the animal replaced its teeth every 40.7 days and had fewer replacement teeth than other diplodocoids.
Garderes and colleagues suggested in 2023 that Bajadasaurus might have had a beak-like structure to support its muzzle, though proof is lacking.
Bajadasaurus is classified as a member of the family Dicraeosauridae.
This family is one of three principal groups within the sauropod subdivision Diplodocoidea.
The animal also belongs to the group Flagellicaudata, which unites dicraeosaurids and diplodocids.
Bajadasaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous epoch, specifically from the Late Berriasian to the Valanginian stages.
It lived between 145 and 132.9 million years ago in northern Patagonia, Argentina.
Fossils date to approximately 140 million years ago during the early Cretaceous period in what is now South America.
The remains were recovered from the Bajada Colorada Formation in northern Patagonia.
It is debated whether the elongated spines served for defense or other functions, though passive defense is one proposed hypothesis.
A 2022 study by Cerda and colleagues challenged the belief that dicraeosaurid spines supported a keratinous sheath, suggesting ligaments instead.
Cerda and colleagues suggested the spine features are consistent with a neck sail used for display or deterrence.
It is debated whether Bajadasaurus had a beak-like structure, as definitive evidence is currently missing.
